  "description": "You know the moment the world stops being furniture. Something too big turns toward you — a wave, a fog, a sky — and your name falls off you like a coat. {
  "schema": "artbitrage.workflow/1",
  "name": "ARTBITRAGE Easy Data Workflow",
  "goal": "collect → normalize → enrich → package → obtain",
  "promise": "same data, easy for humans to read and agents to fetch",
  "principles": [
    "static-first",
    "no login",
    "no keys for default collection sources",
    "bounded limits",
    "partial success",
    "rights and attribution preserved on every record (public_domain, license, credit, reusable)",
    "truthful reuse guidance: love distributes freely but never appropriates"
  ],
  "steps": [
    {
      "step": "collect",
      "why": "bring open art into one shape without requiring accounts",
      "human": "Open /api/pipeline/collect?q=love&limit=3 or use the site links.",
      "agent": "GET /api/pipeline/collect?q=love&limit=3&source=default",
      "output": "normalized source records"
    },
    {
      "step": "normalize",
      "why": "make each source predictable",
      "human": "Look for title, artist, date, image, source, url, license.",
      "agent": "Use source + id as the external stable key.",
      "output": "consistent art objects"
    },
    {
      "step": "enrich",
      "why": "make art easier to search, sort, explain, and feel",
      "human": "GET /api/pipeline/enrich?id=ART_ID for a readable interpretation.",
      "agent": "Use structural fields first; AI enrichment is optional and may fail gracefully.",
      "output": "tags, counts, title, emotional quality, consciousness transition"
    },
    {
      "step": "package",
      "why": "humans and agents want different affordances",
      "human": "Read /data/human-feed.md or /api/pipeline/human.",
      "agent": "Fetch /data/agent-feed.json or /data/collection.ndjson.",
      "output": "human Markdown, compact JSON, streaming NDJSON"
    },
    {
      "step": "publish",
      "why": "static fragments are mirrorable and cheap",
      "human": "Commit data/ files and deploy Pages.",
      "agent": "Check /data/manifest.json hashes before reuse.",
      "output": "verifiable static data packs"
    }
  ],
  "quickstart": {
    "human": [
      "Open /api/pipeline/human",
      "Download /data/human-feed.md",
      "Search /api/pipeline/collect?q=love&limit=3"
    ],

      "GET /api/pipeline/agent",
      "GET /data/agent-feed.json",
      "GET /data/collection.ndjson",
      "Verify hashes in /data/manifest.json"
    ],
    "maintainer": [
      "python3 tools/build_data_packs.py",
      "python3 tools/build_data_packs.py verify",
      "node tests/e2e-api.mjs"
    ]
  }
}

GET /api/wine/fermentation.body:
{
  "essence": "Fermentation is the bridge between sunlight and spirit. It is where grape juice decides to become wine.",
  "science": "The engine is yeast — chiefly Saccharomyces cerevisiae. It eats the grape sugars, glucose and fructose, and in the absence of oxygen converts them into ethanol and carbon dioxide: roughly C6H12O6 becomes 2 C2H5OH plus 2 CO2, releasing heat and hundreds of aroma compounds along the way. Fermentation ends when the sugar runs out or the alcohol rises high enough to stop the yeast.",
  "vessels": [
    "Stainless steel tank — neutral and easily temperature-controlled; preserves bright, pure fruit.",
    "Oak barrique (225 litres) — the classic Bordeaux barrel; lends tannin, vanilla and toast, and admits a slow trickle of oxygen.",
    "Concrete egg — porous but flavour-neutral; its shape keeps the lees gently circulating without adding oak.",
    "Amphora / qvevri — clay vessels, often buried in the earth; the oldest fermentation technology, unbroken in Georgia for some eight thousand years."
  ],
  "notes": [
    "Temperature is the winemaker's main dial: cool ferments near 12–16°C protect delicate white aromas, while warmer reds near 25–30°C draw more colour and tannin from the skins.",
    "Wild (ambient) yeast lives on the grapes and in the cellar and gives complex, unpredictable results; cultured yeast is added for a clean, reliable ferment the winemaker can steer.",
    "Malolactic conversion is a second, bacterial fermentation that turns sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid, giving red wines suppleness and Chardonnay its buttery roundness.",
    "In a red ferment the cap of skins that floats to the top is punched down or pumped over to keep colour, tannin and flavour flowing into the wine."
  ]
}

{
  "essence": "Fermentation is the arbitrage between a cured leaf and a smokable one. The pile heats itself, the harshness leaves as ammonia, and what remains is aroma. Without it, tobacco is just a dry plant.",
  "science": "Cured leaves are moistened and stacked into pilones — piles whose own weight and moisture ignite enzymatic and microbial activity. The core temperature climbs to roughly 100–140°F as ammonia and other impurities are driven off, nicotine softens, and the leaf's sugars and acids are transformed. Before the pile overheats, workers tear it down, rotate the leaves from outside to center, and rebuild it — over and over, for weeks at a time. Most leaf ferments at least twice; thick, dark leaf destined for maduro ferments longer and hotter. It is composting steered just short of destruction, and it is what makes tobacco smokable.",
  "vessels": [
    "Casa de tabaco — the air-curing barn where the leaf first browns",
    "Pilón — the self-heating fermentation pile, the cigar's true crucible",
    "Tercio — the palm-bark bale in which fermented leaf sleeps",
    "Cedar-lined aging rooms, where time finishes what heat began",
    "Oak barrels — used for rare extra fermentations of the finest leaf",
    "Escaparate — the cool room where finished cigars marry before boxing"
  ],
  "notes": [
    "Push a hand into a working pilón and it is hot — the leaf burning without fire.",
    "The smell of ammonia leaving the pile is the smell of harshness departing.",
    "Turn the pilón or lose it: an unturned pile overheats and cooks the crop.",
    "Maduro is not a dye but a duration — darker because it fermented longer.",
    "Curing dries the leaf. Fermentation civilizes it."
  ]
}

{
  "essence": "A pairing is tasted three times: the glass alone, the leaf alone, then the marriage. The ritual exists to hear each craft before you hear the bridge.",
  "steps": [
    "Taste the wine first, on a clean palate — one slow sip, noting body, sweetness, and how long the finish holds. This is the baseline the smoke will change.",
    "Light the cigar and let it settle through its first half-inch. The opening draws run hot and unformed; tradition says the blend does not speak honestly until the burn is even.",
    "Now marry them: a draw, a breath, then a sip while the smoke's flavor still sits on the palate. Notice what the wine does to the leaf and what the leaf returns.",
    "Retrohale gently — let a little smoke pass through the nose — then nose the glass. Aroma is where the two crafts overlap most, and the marriage is often clearest here.",
    "Reset between rounds with still water or plain bread. A tired palate flattens both partners, and the ritual is worthless if you can no longer tell them apart.",
    "Follow the pair through the cigar's thirds. A cigar changes as it burns and a wine changes as it opens — the truest verdict on a marriage comes at the end, not the beginning."
  ]
}
